client: I've been really dreading this family reunion that's coming up next month, and honestly just thinking about it makes my heart race. There was this big fallout with my cousin last year, and I have no idea how to face everyone after that. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something.
therapist: It sounds like even just bringing this up carries a real weight for you — there's a mix of dread and uncertainty in both your words and your voice, and that makes a lot of sense given what happened with your cousin. The fact that you're here and trying, even when part of you doubts it will help, is actually a meaningful first step that's worth acknowledging. Let's gently explore what specifically feels most overwhelming about facing everyone — is it the uncertainty of what might be said, or more the fear of how others might see you after the fallout?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it's more the fear of how they'll see me, honestly. Like, I keep imagining showing up to my aunt's birthday next month and everyone just... looking at me differently, like I'm the one who caused all this drama, even though it was a two-way thing. The uncertainty is there too, but that judgment piece is what keeps me up at night.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quietly, quickly, like you're almost bracing yourself just describing it — really reflects how much that fear of being judged is sitting on you, even right now. What stands out to me is something important you said: *it was a two-way thing* — and yet your mind seems to be casting you as the sole villain in everyone else's eyes, which is worth gently questioning. Can we explore what actual evidence you have that your family sees it that way, versus what your anxious mind might be filling in for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that my mind is just filling in the worst version of things. But the thing is, my sister hasn't really spoken to me properly since it happened, and my mom gets this look on her face when my cousin's name comes up, like she's carefully avoiding something. That feels like pretty real evidence to me, not just my anxiety making stuff up.
therapist: The tension in your voice really comes through — there's a real urgency there, like you need me to understand that this isn't just in your head, and I do hear that. You're right that your sister's distance and your mom's careful avoidance are real things worth taking seriously — but I'd gently invite you to consider whether there might be other explanations for their behavior, like *them* feeling caught in the middle and not knowing what to say, rather than silently blaming you. What do you think it would take to find out what they're actually thinking, rather than having to guess?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe they're just stuck in the middle and don't know what to say. But honestly, the idea of actually asking them what they're thinking terrifies me, because what if I ask and they confirm what I already fear — that they do blame me for what happened with my dad's estate? It feels safer to just keep guessing than to risk hearing something that would make everything so much worse.
therapist: The way you said that — very quietly, almost like you were shrinking into yourself — tells me how much vulnerability is wrapped up in even imagining that conversation. What you're describing is actually a really common but painful trap: the uncertainty feels unbearable, but the potential confirmation feels even worse, so staying in the dark becomes a way of protecting yourself. The hard truth that CBT asks us to sit with, though, is this — right now you're already living with the pain of assuming the worst, so the "safer" option may not actually be protecting you as much as it feels like it is.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows it's true. But knowing something logically and actually being able to act on it are two completely different things for me. Like, right now I'm already hurting, but at least it's a familiar kind of hurt — reaching out to them and getting silence or something cold back would feel like a whole new level of pain that I'm not sure I could handle.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched high, like the words are tumbling out under pressure — tells me this is hitting something really deep and real for you, even as you're trying to reason through it calmly. What you're describing has a name in CBT: it's called "safety behavior," where we choose the familiar pain over the unknown one, not because it actually hurts less, but because it feels more *controllable*. I want to gently ask — how long do you think you can keep carrying this familiar hurt before it starts costing you more than the risk of reaching out ever would?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, the "safety behavior" thing kind of makes sense when you explain it like that. But I've been carrying this loneliness for so long that it almost feels like... I don't know, like it's just part of who I am now, not something I'm choosing. And your question about how long I can keep doing this — it actually scared me a little, because I genuinely don't know the answer.
therapist: The way your voice is carrying that — quick, high, like something just cracked open a little — tells me that question landed somewhere important, and I want to honor that rather than rush past it. What you just said is really significant: when loneliness stops feeling like something happening *to* you and starts feeling like *who you are*, that's often a sign it's been carried alone for far too long. The fact that you don't know how much longer you can do this isn't a scary dead end — it might actually be the first honest opening toward something different.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, but another part of me just feels... tired of hoping that things can be different. Like, I've thought before that maybe something was shifting, and then I just end up back in the same place, eating dinner alone, going to bed alone, wondering if anyone actually noticed I existed that day. I don't know if this is an "opening" or just me finally admitting out loud how bad it's gotten.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, almost like you're speaking from somewhere very far away, makes what you just said feel even more significant — this isn't frustration or panic, it's exhaustion, and that's one of the heaviest things a person can carry. What you're describing — those evenings alone, wondering if anyone noticed you — that's a profound kind of pain, and I want you to know that saying it out loud here, to me, matters. I don't think this is just you admitting how bad it's gotten — I think this is you deciding, maybe for the first time in a while, that you deserve to be heard.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know if I'd go that far — saying I "deserve" to be heard feels like a big leap when most of the time I just feel like a burden to people. But something about saying it out loud did feel different, like I'd been carrying this weight in silence for so long that even just naming it made it slightly more real. I just don't want to get my hopes up that talking about it will actually change anything.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice — almost like you're rushing to qualify what you just felt before it can mean too much — tells me that even allowing yourself a moment of relief feels risky, like hope itself is something to be guarded against. And that belief that you're a burden — I want to gently name that as one of the most painful and also most *questionable* thoughts you've shared today, because it's the kind of thought that feels absolutely true from the inside while quietly closing every door around you. You don't have to believe you deserve to be heard yet — but I'd ask you to just stay open to the possibility that the voice telling you you're a burden might not be the most reliable narrator of your story.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but that voice has been there so long it basically feels like... me. Like, how do I separate what's a distorted thought from just knowing myself? And honestly, every time I've let myself believe I wasn't a burden, something happened to prove me wrong again.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but fast, almost like you're bracing for this thought to be dismissed too — tells me this question comes from somewhere very worn down, not just curious. What you're describing is actually one of the most important questions in this kind of work: when a painful belief has been with us long enough, it stops feeling like *a thought we have* and starts feeling like *the truth we are* — but the fact that you can even ask "how do I separate them?" suggests some part of you already senses the difference. Those moments where something "proved you right" — I'd gently invite you to look at whether life was confirming the truth, or whether that belief was quietly shaping which moments you noticed and remembered.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true — that the belief has been filtering what I notice, not just confirming reality. But honestly, it's hard not to feel like that's just a clever way of talking me out of something that feels really real to me, you know? Like, what if the belief is accurate and I've just been alone because people genuinely don't want to stay around me?
therapist: The softness in your voice, pitched high but almost fragile, tells me this isn't resistance — it's something more like a quiet, exhausted plea to not have your reality taken away from you, and I want to honor that. You're asking one of the most honest and painful questions a person can ask, and I'm not going to talk you out of it with cleverness — but I will ask you this: if a close friend came to you and said "people don't stay because I'm genuinely unlovable," would you look at the evidence the same way you're looking at your own? The goal isn't to convince you the pain isn't real — it absolutely is — but to gently question whether "people have left" and "I am someone people don't want" are actually the same conclusion.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
